title: NASA Challenges College Students to Design the Future of Lunar Living
summary: What will it take for humans to live and work on the Moon? NASA is turning to college students for answers. The 2027 Revolutionary Aerospace Systems Concepts - Academic Linkage (RASC-AL) competition invites U.S.-based collegiate teams to submit original concepts that could shape a future lunar outpost, particularly in the challenging South Pole region. This area is scientifically intriguing because some craters are permanently shadowed, potentially harboring water ice—a crucial resource for long-term habitation. The competition, running since 2002, bridges academia, NASA, and industry to foster innovation. This year's themes include prospecting in shadowed craters and developing expandable infrastructure for astronauts. 'This competition showcases the technical excellence and creativity of the next generation of explorers and innovators,' said Chris Jones, chief technologist at NASA's Langley Research Center. Teams must submit a notice of intent by October 13, with full proposals due February 24, 2027. Up to 14 finalist teams will receive $7,500 each and present their concepts at the RASC-AL Forum in Cocoa Beach, Florida, in June 2027. The top two teams earn additional awards and a chance to present at a major aerospace conference. For students passionate about space, this is a rare opportunity to contribute directly to NASA's mission and maybe even shape how humanity returns to the Moon.
why_it_matters: The competition matters because student concepts could influence real lunar habitats, resource use, and the next phase of human spaceflight. It also shows how public agencies use open challenges to build a skilled workforce while solving problems they cannot solve alone.

background_read: NASA's Langley Research Center, located in Hampton, Virginia, is one of the agency's oldest field centers and has contributed to projects from early space capsules to lunar landing research.
The RASC-AL competition has been running since 2002 as a bridge between university engineering programs and NASA mission planners, often focusing on Moon and Mars exploration.

The lunar South Pole is a particularly difficult environment: some crater floors are permanently shadowed, so temperatures stay extremely low and water ice may have survived there for billions of years.
NASA's Artemis program, the current effort to return astronauts to the Moon, is targeting that same region because ice could supply water, oxygen, and rocket fuel.

By asking students to design prospecting and expandable infrastructure systems, the competition turns open-ended academic work into proposals NASA may seriously consider; Chris Jones, the chief technologist at Langley, said the goal is to showcase the next generation of explorers and innovators.

perspectives.description: They gain fresh, low-cost ideas from students and build a pipeline of future engineers. The competition helps NASA test concepts for lunar South Pole operations that may feed into Artemis and later missions.

They get a rare chance to work on real spaceflight problems and win money and visibility, but the workload is intense and only a small number of teams become finalists. Smaller or less-resourced universities may struggle to compete.

They see RASC-AL as a long-running example of how open design challenges can bridge academia, NASA, and industry. The challenge is measuring whether student concepts actually influence missions or mainly serve as educational experiences.

They want the competition to produce practical tools for prospecting water ice and building expandable habitats, because those capabilities could support a lasting human presence. The next step is testing these ideas in simulated or real lunar conditions.
